chapter.title: Computer Overview
chapter.summary: This chapter introduces what a computer is and how it developed from simple counting aids to modern machines. It explains the functional units of a computer, the types of memory, the units used to measure memory and data, and how data is captured, stored and retrieved.

content.hinglish: Computer ka safar bahut lamba raha hai. Sabse pehle log ginti ke liye abacus jaise simple tool use karte the. 1642 mein Blaise Pascal ne Pascaline banaya jo jodna-ghatana kar sakta tha. Charles Babbage ko 'Father of Computer' kaha jata hai kyunki unhone Analytical Engine design kiya. 1946 mein ENIAC pehla bada electronic computer tha jo vacuum tubes par chalta tha. Aaj ke computer Artificial Intelligence aur parallel processing use karte hain, isi ko fifth generation kehte hain.
content.formalDefinition: The evolution of computers refers to the gradual development of computing devices from simple manual calculating aids such as the abacus to modern high-speed electronic machines. It is broadly divided into five generations, each defined by a major change in the main electronic component used: vacuum tubes, transistors, integrated circuits, microprocessors, and artificial intelligence. With every generation, computers became smaller, faster, cheaper and capable of storing more data.
examples: Abacus used for counting in ancient times
Pascaline mechanical adding machine built by Blaise Pascal
ENIAC, the first large electronic computer (1946)
Modern laptop running on a microprocessor
Smartphones with AI-based voice assistants

tables.title: Five Generations of Computers
rows: Very large, high heat, machine language; e.g. ENIAC, UNIVAC
Smaller, faster, less heat; assembly language; e.g. IBM 1401
More reliable, keyboard and monitor used; high-level languages; e.g. IBM 360
Personal computers, GUI, networks; e.g. IBM PC, Apple Macintosh
Parallel processing, voice recognition, AI; e.g. IBM Watson

diagrams:
Timeline of Computer Evolution
1620s  Abacus (manual counting)
1642   Pascaline (Blaise Pascal)
1671   Stepped Reckoner (Leibniz)
1837   Analytical Engine (Charles Babbage)
1890   Hollerith's Tabulating Machine
1946   ENIAC (vacuum tubes)
1948   Transistor invented
1958   Integrated Circuit (IC)
1971   Microprocessor (Intel 4004)
Present AI-based computers

differences.title: Difference between the Abacus and a Modern Computer

commonMistakes: Thinking Charles Babbage invented the abacus; he designed the Analytical Engine.
Calling ENIAC the first mechanical calculator; it was the first large electronic computer.
Mixing up generations, e.g. putting transistors in the first generation instead of the second.
Assuming the fifth generation is only about speed; its defining feature is Artificial Intelligence.
examNotes: Blaise Pascal invented the Pascaline (1642), a mechanical adding machine.
Charles Babbage is called the 'Father of the Computer' for designing the Analytical Engine.
ENIAC (1946) used vacuum tubes and is called the first large electronic computer.
Each generation is identified by its main electronic component.
Second generation used transistors; the third used integrated circuits.
The fourth generation introduced microprocessors and personal computers.

faqs.q: Who invented the first mechanical calculator?
faqs.a: Blaise Pascal invented the Pascaline in 1642, a mechanical machine that could add and subtract.

faqs.q: Why is Charles Babbage called the Father of the Computer?
faqs.a: He designed the Analytical Engine, the first machine with the idea of a stored program and a separate processing unit, which is the basis of modern computers.

faqs.q: What defines a computer generation?
faqs.a: A generation is defined by the main electronic component used, such as vacuum tubes, transistors, integrated circuits, microprocessors or artificial intelligence.

faqs.q: Which was the first large electronic computer?
faqs.a: ENIAC (Electronic Numerical Integrator And Computer), built in 1946, was the first large electronic computer and used vacuum tubes.

quiz.question: Who is known as the Father of the Computer?
quiz.explanation: Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine, the first machine with the concept of a stored program, so he is called the Father of the Computer.

quiz.question: Which component was used in first generation computers?
quiz.explanation: First generation computers such as ENIAC used vacuum tubes as their main electronic component.

quiz.question: Microprocessors were introduced in which generation?
quiz.explanation: The fourth generation (1971 onwards) used microprocessors and gave rise to personal computers.

quiz.question: ENIAC was developed in the year:
quiz.explanation: ENIAC was completed in 1946 and was the first large electronic computer.

checklist: I can name the key inventors and their machines (Pascal, Babbage, Hollerith).
I can list the five generations and their main components.
I can explain why Babbage is called the Father of the Computer.
I can state the year and importance of ENIAC.
I can describe how size, speed and cost changed across generations.

content.hinglish: Computer ke andar kai units milkar kaam karte hain. Input unit bahar se data aur instructions leta hai, jaise keyboard se. CPU computer ka dimaag hota hai jisme ALU aur Control Unit hote hain. ALU arithmetic aur logical operations karta hai, aur Control Unit sab units ko control karta hai. Memory data aur instructions store karti hai, aur Output unit result ko screen ya printer par dikhata hai. In sab units ko milkar functional units kehte hain.
content.formalDefinition: The functional units of a computer are the basic building blocks that together perform the complete cycle of accepting data, processing it and producing output. They are the Input Unit, the Central Processing Unit (CPU) consisting of the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU), the Control Unit (CU) and registers, the Memory Unit, and the Output Unit. Each unit performs a specific function, and all units work together under the control of the CPU.
examples: Keyboard and mouse as input units
Monitor and printer as output units
ALU adding two numbers entered by the user
Control Unit fetching and decoding instructions
RAM storing the currently running program

tables.title: Functional Units and Their Functions
rows: Accepts data and instructions from the user
Controls and coordinates all units; fetches and decodes instructions
Temporary high-speed storage inside the CPU
Presents the processed result to the user

differences.title: Difference between the ALU and the Control Unit
rows: Directs the flow of data and controls all units
Decides which instruction to execute next

commonMistakes: Saying the CPU is only the ALU; the CPU also contains the Control Unit and registers.
Confusing the Control Unit with the whole computer; it is only a part of the CPU.
Thinking the memory unit is not a functional unit; it is a core part of the computer.
Believing the input unit processes data; it only supplies data to the CPU.
examNotes: The four main functional units are the input unit, CPU, memory unit and output unit.
The CPU has three parts: ALU, Control Unit and registers.
The ALU performs arithmetic (+,-,*,/) and logical (<,>,=) operations.
The Control Unit is called the nerve centre because it coordinates all units.
In Von Neumann architecture, both data and instructions are stored in the same memory.
The input unit converts human-readable data into a computer-readable form.

faqs.q: Which part of the CPU does calculations?
faqs.a: The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) performs all arithmetic and logical operations.

faqs.q: Why is the Control Unit called the nerve centre?
faqs.a: It controls and coordinates the working of all other units by fetching, decoding and directing instructions.

faqs.q: What are registers?
faqs.a: Registers are very small, very fast storage locations inside the CPU used to hold data and instructions temporarily during processing.

faqs.q: What is Von Neumann architecture?
faqs.a: It is a design in which both data and instructions are stored in the same main memory and are fetched and executed one at a time by the CPU.

quiz.question: Which unit performs arithmetic and logical operations?
quiz.explanation: The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) is responsible for all arithmetic and logical operations.

quiz.question: Which unit is called the nerve centre of the computer?
quiz.explanation: The Control Unit coordinates and controls all the units, so it is called the nerve centre.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a part of the CPU?
quiz.explanation: A hard disk is secondary memory; the CPU consists of the ALU, Control Unit and registers.

quiz.question: The CPU is also known as the:
quiz.explanation: The CPU is also called the processor because it processes all the data and instructions.

checklist: I can name and describe all four functional units.
I can list the three parts of the CPU.
I can explain the function of the ALU and the Control Unit.
I can draw a block diagram of a computer.
I can explain Von Neumann architecture in one line.

content.hinglish: Memory ka kaam data aur instructions ko store karna hai. Primary memory computer ke andar hoti hai, jaise RAM aur ROM. RAM volatile hoti hai, matlab power off hone par uska data chala jata hai, jabki ROM non-volatile hoti hai. Secondary memory jaise hard disk aur pen drive permanent storage ke liye use hoti hai. Cache memory bahut fast hoti hai aur CPU aur main memory ke beech rakhi jati hai.
content.formalDefinition: Computer memory is the storage area that holds data, instructions and results. It is classified into primary memory (main memory) and secondary memory (auxiliary memory). Primary memory, such as RAM and ROM, is directly accessible to the CPU; RAM is volatile while ROM is non-volatile. Secondary memory, such as hard disks, SSDs and pen drives, is non-volatile, cheaper and used for permanent storage. Registers and cache are the fastest memories located closest to the CPU.
examples: RAM storing the program that is currently running
ROM storing the BIOS or firmware of a computer
Hard disk storing files, photos and movies
Pen drive used to transfer data between computers
Cache memory speeding up repeated CPU access

tables.title: Primary vs Secondary Memory
rows: Hard disk, SSD, Pen drive, DVD

diagrams:
Memory Hierarchy (fastest and smallest at the top)

            CPU
             |
        Registers (fastest, smallest)
             |
           Cache
             |
     Main Memory (RAM / ROM)
             |
  Secondary Memory (HDD / SSD / DVD)
             |
   Tertiary / Cloud Storage (slowest, largest)
commonMistakes: Saying RAM is non-volatile; RAM is volatile and loses its contents when power is switched off.
Thinking ROM can be freely written to; ROM is normally read-only.
Confusing cache memory with the main memory (RAM).
Assuming secondary memory is directly accessed by the CPU; it is not.
examNotes: Memory is divided into primary memory and secondary memory.
RAM is volatile; ROM is non-volatile.
RAM is of two types: SRAM (static) and DRAM (dynamic).
ROM is of three types: PROM, EPROM and EEPROM.
Cache memory sits between the CPU and main memory to increase speed.
Secondary memory is non-volatile and used for permanent storage.

faqs.q: Why is RAM called volatile memory?
faqs.a: RAM loses all its contents when the power is switched off, so it is called volatile memory.

faqs.q: What is stored in ROM?
faqs.a: ROM stores permanent instructions such as the BIOS or firmware needed to start (boot) the computer.

faqs.q: What is cache memory?
faqs.a: Cache is a small, very fast memory placed between the CPU and the main memory that stores frequently used data to speed up processing.

faqs.q: Give two examples of secondary memory.
faqs.a: Hard disk drive (HDD) and Solid State Drive (SSD) are examples of secondary memory. A pen drive is another example.

quiz.question: Which memory is volatile?
quiz.explanation: RAM is volatile; it loses its data when power is switched off, unlike ROM and secondary storage.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a secondary storage device?
quiz.explanation: An SSD is a secondary storage device; RAM, ROM and cache are primary memory.

quiz.question: ROM stands for:
quiz.explanation: ROM stands for Read Only Memory, which is non-volatile and normally read-only.

quiz.question: Which memory is fastest?
quiz.explanation: Registers are inside the CPU and are the fastest and smallest type of memory.

checklist: I can classify memory into primary and secondary.
I can explain volatile and non-volatile memory with examples.
I can list the types of RAM and ROM.
I can describe the role of cache memory.
I can draw and explain the memory hierarchy.

content.hinglish: Computer mein data chhote units mein store hota hai. Sabse chhoti unit bit hoti hai jo 0 ya 1 ho sakti hai. Aath bits milkar ek byte bante hain, aur chaar bits ko nibble kehte hain. 1024 bytes = 1 kilobyte, 1024 KB = 1 megabyte, 1024 MB = 1 gigabyte aur 1024 GB = 1 terabyte. Dhyan rahe ki storage banane wali companies decimal system (1000) bhi use karti hain, isliye 500 GB ki drive thodi kam dikhti hai.
content.formalDefinition: The basic units of measurement in computers express the size of data and memory. The smallest unit is the bit, which stores a single binary digit 0 or 1. A group of 8 bits forms a byte, and 4 bits form a nibble. Larger units are formed using powers of 1024 in the binary convention: 1 KB = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB, 1 GB = 1024 MB, 1 TB = 1024 GB and 1 PB = 1024 TB. Storage manufacturers often use the decimal convention where 1 KB = 1000 bytes.
examples: One character of text stored as 1 byte
A small text document of about 10 KB
A song file of about 5 MB
A movie file of about 1.5 GB
A hard disk of 1 TB capacity

tables.title: Units of Memory Measurement (Binary convention, 1 KB = 1024 bytes)

content.pythonSyntax:
# Convert between memory units (binary convention)
size_kb = size_mb * 1024
size_mb = size_gb * 1024
bits = number_of_bytes * 8

codeExamples.explanation: 5 MB is converted to KB by multiplying by 1024, using the binary convention 1 MB = 1024 KB.
2 GB equals 2048 MB because 1 GB = 1024 MB in the binary convention.

differences.title: Difference between Binary and Decimal Memory Conventions

commonMistakes: Writing 1 KB = 1000 bytes when using the binary convention (it is 1024 bytes).
Forgetting that 1 byte = 8 bits, not 10 bits.
Confusing a nibble (4 bits) with a byte (8 bits).
Mixing decimal and binary conventions silently; always state which convention is used.
examNotes: The bit is the smallest unit of memory and stores 0 or 1.
1 byte = 8 bits and 1 nibble = 4 bits.
In the binary convention 1 KB = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB, 1 GB = 1024 MB.
1 TB = 1024 GB and 1 PB = 1024 TB.
Storage manufacturers use the decimal convention (1 KB = 1000 bytes).
Always mention the convention used when converting units in an exam.

faqs.q: What is a bit?
faqs.a: A bit (binary digit) is the smallest unit of memory and can store either 0 or 1.

faqs.q: How many bits are there in a byte?
faqs.a: One byte contains 8 bits.

faqs.q: Why does a 500 GB drive show less space?
faqs.a: Manufacturers use the decimal convention (1 GB = 1000^3 bytes) while the operating system uses the binary convention (1 GiB = 1024^3 bytes), so the shown capacity is smaller.

faqs.q: What is the largest unit listed here?
faqs.a: Among the units listed, the petabyte (PB) is the largest, equal to 1024 TB.

quiz.question: How many bits are there in one byte?
quiz.explanation: One byte consists of 8 bits.

quiz.question: 1 KB equals how many bytes in the binary convention?
quiz.explanation: In the binary convention 1 KB = 1024 bytes (2^10 bytes).

quiz.question: A nibble consists of:
quiz.explanation: A nibble is a group of 4 bits, which is half a byte.

quiz.question: 1 GB equals how many MB (binary convention)?
quiz.explanation: 1 GB = 1024 MB in the binary convention.

checklist: I can list the memory units from bit to petabyte.
I can state that 1 byte = 8 bits and 1 nibble = 4 bits.
I can convert between KB, MB, GB and TB.
I can explain the binary and decimal conventions.
I can solve simple memory conversion problems.

content.hinglish: Data capturing ka matlab hai raw data ko computer mein daalna. Iske liye keyboard, mouse aur scanner jaise devices use hote hain. Kuch special devices bhi hote hain: OMR answer sheets ke marks padhta hai, OCR printed text ko digital text banata hai, aur MICR bank cheques ke numbers padhta hai. Data ko hard disk ya pen drive mein store kiya jata hai. Jab zarurat pade to stored data ko wapas nikalna retrieval kehlata hai.
content.formalDefinition: Data capturing is the process of collecting and entering raw data into a computer system using input devices. Storage is the process of saving this captured data on primary or secondary storage media for future use, and retrieval is the process of locating and bringing back the stored data when required. Common data capturing devices include the keyboard, mouse, scanner, barcode reader, OMR, OCR, MICR and biometric sensors.
examples: Typing marks into a spreadsheet using a keyboard
Scanning a barcode at a supermarket checkout
OMR checking of an objective answer sheet
MICR reading cheque numbers in a bank
Fingerprint scanner used for attendance

tables.title: Common Data Capturing Devices
rows: Converting printed documents into digital form
Reading pencil marks on objective answer sheets
Converting scanned text images into editable text
Reading magnetic ink characters on bank cheques
Capturing fingerprints or iris for identification

codeExamples.explanation: Raw marks (data) are processed to give meaningful information (the average).

commonMistakes: Confusing data (raw facts) with information (processed data).
Mixing up OCR and OMR; OCR reads text, OMR reads pencil marks.
Thinking MICR is used to read barcodes; MICR is used on bank cheques.
Believing that retrieval means deleting data; it means bringing stored data back.
examNotes: Data are raw facts; information is processed, meaningful data.
Data capturing means entering raw data using input devices.
OMR reads pencil marks, OCR reads printed text, MICR reads magnetic ink characters.
Barcode readers are widely used in shops and libraries.
Storage saves data for future use; retrieval brings stored data back when needed.
Biometric devices capture fingerprints or iris patterns for identification.

faqs.q: What is the difference between data and information?
faqs.a: Data are raw unprocessed facts, while information is the meaningful result obtained after processing the data.

faqs.q: Where is MICR used?
faqs.a: MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition) is used in banks to read the magnetic ink numbers printed on cheques.

faqs.q: What does OMR stand for?
faqs.a: OMR stands for Optical Mark Recognition, used to read pencil marks on objective answer sheets.

faqs.q: What is retrieval?
faqs.a: Retrieval is the process of locating and bringing back stored data from memory or storage when it is needed.

quiz.question: Which device reads pencil marks on answer sheets?
quiz.explanation: OMR (Optical Mark Recognition) reads the pencil marks made on objective answer sheets.

quiz.question: MICR is mainly used in:
quiz.explanation: MICR is used in banks to read the magnetic ink characters on cheques.

quiz.question: Which device is used to capture live video into a computer?
quiz.explanation: A webcam is an input device used to capture live video into the computer.

quiz.question: Raw unprocessed facts are called:
quiz.explanation: Raw unprocessed facts are called data; after processing they become information.

checklist: I can define data capturing, storage and retrieval.
I can distinguish between data and information.
I can list and describe OMR, OCR, MICR and barcode readers.
I can give real-life examples of data capturing devices.
I can explain why storage and retrieval are important.

questions.question: Who is known as the Father of the Computer?
optionExplanations: Blaise Pascal invented the Pascaline, a mechanical adding machine, but is not called the Father of the Computer.
Correct. Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine, the basis of the modern computer, so he is called the Father of the Computer.
Herman Hollerith developed the tabulating machine for the census, not the first general computer design.
John von Neumann gave the stored-program concept, but is not called the Father of the Computer.
questions.explanation: Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine, which first introduced the idea of a separate processing unit and stored instructions. Because modern computers follow this design, he is called the Father of the Computer.

questions.question: Which electronic component was used in first generation computers?
optionExplanations: Transistors were used in second generation computers, not the first.
Integrated circuits were used in third generation computers.
Correct. First generation computers such as ENIAC used vacuum tubes.
Microprocessors were used in fourth generation computers.
questions.explanation: Each computer generation is defined by its main electronic component. The first generation (1940-1956) used vacuum tubes, which were large, generated a lot of heat and consumed much power.

questions.question: ENIAC stands for:
optionExplanations: Correct. ENIAC stands for Electronic Numerical Integrator And Computer.
This is a made-up expansion; ENIAC does not stand for Electronic Number Input And Calculator.
The words are rearranged; the correct expansion is Electronic Numerical Integrator And Computer.
This is incorrect; ENIAC is not a network interface device.
questions.explanation: ENIAC, the Electronic Numerical Integrator And Computer, was built in 1946. It was the first large electronic computer and used vacuum tubes.

questions.question: The microprocessor was introduced in which generation of computers?
optionExplanations: The first generation used vacuum tubes, not microprocessors.
The second generation used transistors.
The third generation used integrated circuits.
Correct. The fourth generation (1971 onwards) introduced microprocessors and personal computers.
questions.explanation: The fourth generation began with the invention of the microprocessor, which put an entire CPU on a single chip. This made personal computers possible.

questions.question: Herman Hollerith's tabulating machine was mainly developed for:
optionExplanations: Hollerith's machine was not used for weather forecasting.
Correct. It was developed to speed up counting for the US census.
It was not designed for banking transactions.
It had no connection with space research.
questions.explanation: Herman Hollerith built a tabulating machine using punched cards to process the US census data quickly. His company later grew into IBM.

questions.question: Which unit of the CPU performs arithmetic and logical operations?
optionExplanations: The Control Unit controls operations but does not perform calculations.
The Memory Unit stores data but does not process it.
Correct. The ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) performs all arithmetic and logical operations.
The Output Unit only presents results; it does not compute.
questions.explanation: The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) carries out arithmetic operations like addition and subtraction, and logical operations like comparison, inside the CPU.

questions.question: Which unit coordinates and controls all other units of a computer?
optionExplanations: The ALU performs calculations but does not control other units.
Correct. The Control Unit coordinates and controls all units, so it is called the nerve centre.
The Input Unit only supplies data to the computer.
Registers store data temporarily but do not control the system.
questions.explanation: The Control Unit fetches instructions, decodes them and directs all other units to carry out the required operations, acting as the nerve centre of the computer.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a part of the CPU?
optionExplanations: The ALU is a part of the CPU.
The Control Unit is a part of the CPU.
Registers are located inside the CPU.
Correct. A hard disk is secondary memory, not a part of the CPU.
questions.explanation: The CPU consists of the ALU, the Control Unit and registers. A hard disk is a secondary storage device, so it is not part of the CPU.

questions.question: The CPU is also known as the:
optionExplanations: Memory is a separate functional unit; the CPU is not memory.
Correct. The CPU is also called the processor because it processes data and instructions.
An output device presents results; the CPU is not an output device.
The CPU processes data; storage is done by memory units.
questions.explanation: The Central Processing Unit is also called the processor because it processes all the data and instructions of a program.

questions.question: Which unit converts the processed result into a human-readable form?
optionExplanations: The Input Unit brings data in; it does not present results.
The Memory Unit stores data but does not display results.
Correct. The Output Unit converts processed results into a human-readable form.
The ALU performs calculations but does not present the result.
questions.explanation: The Output Unit, such as a monitor or printer, converts the processed result into a form that the user can understand and use.

questions.question: Which of the following is a volatile memory?
optionExplanations: ROM is non-volatile; it keeps its contents when power is off.
Correct. RAM is volatile and loses its contents when power is switched off.
A hard disk is non-volatile secondary memory.
A DVD is non-volatile secondary storage.
questions.explanation: Volatile memory loses its contents when power is switched off. RAM is volatile, while ROM and secondary storage devices are non-volatile.

questions.question: Which of the following is a secondary storage device?
optionExplanations: RAM is primary memory, not secondary storage.
Cache is a fast primary memory inside or near the CPU.
Correct. An SSD (Solid State Drive) is a secondary storage device.
Registers are the fastest primary memory inside the CPU.
questions.explanation: Secondary storage devices store data permanently and are not directly accessed by the CPU. An SSD is a secondary storage device, unlike RAM, cache and registers.

questions.question: ROM stands for:
optionExplanations: ROM does not stand for Random Only Memory.
Correct. ROM stands for Read Only Memory.
This is a made-up expansion.
ROM is not called Read Once Memory.
questions.explanation: ROM stands for Read Only Memory. It is non-volatile and normally stores permanent instructions such as the firmware or BIOS.

questions.question: Which memory is non-volatile and stores the firmware or BIOS?
optionExplanations: RAM is volatile and does not store firmware.
Cache is a fast temporary memory used for active data.
Correct. ROM is non-volatile and stores the firmware or BIOS.
Registers hold data only during processing and are not permanent.
questions.explanation: ROM is non-volatile memory that permanently stores the firmware or BIOS, the instructions needed to start (boot) the computer.

questions.question: Which memory is the fastest and located closest to the CPU?
optionExplanations: Correct. Registers are inside the CPU and are the fastest memory.
RAM is fast but slower than registers.
A hard disk is much slower secondary storage.
A DVD is slow secondary storage.
questions.explanation: Registers are small, very fast storage locations inside the CPU. In the memory hierarchy, they are the fastest and smallest memory.

questions.question: How many bits make one byte?
optionExplanations: 2 bits is not a byte.
4 bits form a nibble, not a byte.
Correct. One byte consists of 8 bits.
16 bits make two bytes.
questions.explanation: A byte is a group of 8 bits. It is the standard unit used to store one character of text.

questions.question: 1 kilobyte equals how many bytes in the binary convention?
optionExplanations: 100 is far too small.
1000 bytes is the decimal convention, not the binary one.
Correct. In the binary convention 1 KB = 1024 bytes.
2048 bytes equals 2 KB.
questions.explanation: In the binary convention, 1 KB = 1024 bytes (that is 2^10). Storage manufacturers, however, use the decimal convention where 1 KB = 1000 bytes.

questions.question: Which is the smallest unit of memory?
optionExplanations: A byte is made of 8 bits, so it is not the smallest.
Correct. The bit is the smallest unit of memory.
A nibble is 4 bits, larger than a bit.
A kilobyte is 1024 bytes, much larger than a bit.
questions.explanation: The bit (binary digit) is the smallest unit of memory and stores a single 0 or 1. All larger units are built from bits.

questions.question: 1 megabyte equals how many kilobytes (binary convention)?
optionExplanations: 100 KB is far too small.
1000 KB is the decimal convention, not the binary one.
Correct. In the binary convention 1 MB = 1024 KB.
512 KB is half a megabyte.
questions.explanation: In the binary convention, 1 MB = 1024 KB. The same power-of-1024 pattern continues for GB and TB.

questions.question: A nibble consists of how many bits?
optionExplanations: 2 bits is not a nibble.
Correct. A nibble is a group of 4 bits.
8 bits form a byte, not a nibble.
16 bits make two bytes.
questions.explanation: A nibble is a group of 4 bits, which is exactly half of a byte.

questions.question: Which device is used to read pencil marks on objective answer sheets?
optionExplanations: OCR reads printed text, not pencil marks.
Correct. OMR (Optical Mark Recognition) reads pencil marks on answer sheets.
MICR reads magnetic ink characters on cheques.
A barcode reader reads barcodes on products.
questions.explanation: OMR stands for Optical Mark Recognition. It senses the presence of a pencil mark in a given position, so it is used to check objective answer sheets.

questions.question: MICR technology is mainly used in:
optionExplanations: Supermarkets mainly use barcode readers.
Correct. MICR is used in banks to read the magnetic ink characters on cheques.
Libraries typically use barcode readers or RFID.
Hospitals use various devices, but MICR is specific to banks.
questions.explanation: MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition) reads characters printed with magnetic ink. Banks use it to process cheque numbers quickly and accurately.

questions.question: Which device is used to capture data from the barcode on a product?
optionExplanations: A plotter is an output device for drawings.
Correct. A barcode reader scans and reads the barcode on a product.
A speaker is an output device for sound.
A printer is an output device.
questions.explanation: A barcode reader uses light to scan the black-and-white pattern of a barcode and converts it into digital data, widely used in shops and libraries.

questions.question: OCR is used to:
options: Read pencil marks on answer sheets
Convert scanned printed text into editable text
optionExplanations: Reading pencil marks is done by OMR, not OCR.
Correct. OCR converts a scanned image of printed text into editable text.
Reading magnetic ink on cheques is done by MICR.
Printing is an output task, not OCR.
questions.explanation: OCR (Optical Character Recognition) analyses a scanned image of printed or typed text and converts it into machine-editable text that can be stored and edited.

questions.question: Which of the following is used to capture live video into a computer?
optionExplanations: A printer is an output device.
Correct. A webcam is an input device used to capture live video.
A plotter is an output device for large drawings.
A monitor is an output device that displays information.
questions.explanation: A webcam is an input device that captures live video and images and sends them to the computer for processing or storage.

questions.question: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the correct option.
questions.reason: RAM loses all its contents when the power is switched off.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true and the reason correctly explains the assertion. RAM is called volatile precisely because it loses its stored data when power is switched off.

questions.question: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: The CPU is called the brain of the computer.
questions.reason: The CPU processes data and controls all the other units of the computer.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. The CPU is called the brain because it performs all processing and controls the working of every other unit.

questions.question: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the correct option.
questions.reason: In the binary convention one kilobyte equals 1024 bytes.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: The assertion is false because in the binary convention (used for RAM and by operating systems) 1 KB = 1024 bytes. The reason is true. Hence A is false but R is true.

questions.question: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: A transistor is smaller and more reliable than a vacuum tube.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion. Transistors replaced vacuum tubes in the second generation because they were smaller, faster, more reliable and generated less heat.

questions.question: ENIAC used transistors as its main electronic component.
questions.correction: ENIAC used vacuum tubes as its main electronic component; transistors were used in second generation computers.
questions.explanation: ENIAC (1946) belongs to the first generation, which used vacuum tubes. Transistors came later, in the second generation.

questions.question: RAM is a non-volatile memory.
questions.correction: RAM is a volatile memory; it loses its contents when the power is switched off.
questions.explanation: RAM is volatile memory. It keeps data only while power is on, which is why unsaved work is lost when a computer shuts down unexpectedly.

questions.question: One byte consists of eight bits.
questions.explanation: A byte is defined as a group of 8 bits and is the standard unit for storing one character.

questions.question: The ALU is a part of the CPU.
questions.explanation: The CPU consists of the Arithmetic Logic Unit, the Control Unit and registers, so the ALU is indeed a part of the CPU.

questions.question: MICR is used in banks to read the magnetic ink characters on cheques.
questions.explanation: MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition) reads characters printed with magnetic ink and is widely used by banks for processing cheques.

questions.question: ROM can be freely written by the user during normal operation.
questions.correction: ROM is normally read-only; it cannot be freely written by the user during normal operation.
questions.explanation: ROM stands for Read Only Memory. It is normally read-only and stores permanent instructions such as firmware; special devices are needed to change its contents.

questions.question: The first generation of computers used ______ as the main electronic component.
questions.explanation: First generation computers used vacuum tubes, which were large and produced a lot of heat.

questions.question: The ______ is called the brain of the computer.
questions.explanation: The CPU (Central Processing Unit) processes all data and controls every other unit, so it is called the brain of the computer.

questions.question: 1 kilobyte = ______ bytes in the binary convention.
questions.explanation: In the binary convention 1 KB = 1024 bytes (2^10). The decimal convention would give 1000 bytes.

questions.question: ______ memory loses its contents when the power is switched off.
questions.explanation: Volatile memory, such as RAM, loses its contents when power is switched off.

questions.question: A ______ reader is used to read the barcode printed on a product.
questions.explanation: A barcode reader scans the black-and-white pattern of a barcode and converts it into digital data.

questions.question: The ______ unit converts the processed data into a human-readable form.
questions.explanation: The output unit, such as a monitor or printer, presents the processed result in a form the user can understand.

questions.question: Match the component in Column A with its correct function in Column B.

matchPairs.right: Fast memory between the CPU and RAM

questions.explanation: Each component has a specific role: the ALU computes, the Control Unit coordinates, RAM is volatile main memory, ROM is non-volatile and cache speeds up access between CPU and RAM.

questions.question: Match the memory unit in Column A with its value in Column B (binary convention).
questions.explanation: Memory units grow by a factor of 1024 in the binary convention: 4 bits make a nibble, 8 bits make a byte, and each larger unit is 1024 times the previous one.

questions.question: How many bits are there in 64 bytes?
questions.explanation: Using the relation 1 byte = 8 bits, 64 bytes = 64 x 8 = 512 bits.

questions.question: Convert 3072 KB into MB using the binary convention (1 MB = 1024 KB).
questions.explanation: Binary convention: 1 MB = 1024 KB. So 3072 KB = 3072 / 1024 = 3 MB.

questions.question: A pen drive has a capacity of 16 GB. How many photos of 4 MB each can it store? Use the binary convention (1 GB = 1024 MB).
questions.explanation: Binary convention: 16 GB = 16 x 1024 = 16384 MB. Number of photos = 16384 / 4 = 4096 photos.

questions.question: The RAM of a computer is 8 GB. Express this in megabytes using the binary convention (1 GB = 1024 MB).
questions.explanation: Binary convention: 8 GB = 8 x 1024 = 8192 MB.

questions.question: A manufacturer sells a 1 TB drive using the decimal convention (1 TB = 10^12 bytes). Approximately how many gibibytes (GiB) is this, if 1 GiB = 2^30 bytes? Round to the nearest whole number.
questions.explanation: Decimal convention: 1 TB = 1,000,000,000,000 bytes. Binary convention: 1 GiB = 2^30 = 1,073,741,824 bytes. So 1,000,000,000,000 / 1,073,741,824 = 931.32, which rounds to 931 GiB. This is why a '1 TB' drive shows less space in the operating system.

questions.question: What is a computer?
questions.modelAnswer: A computer is an electronic device that accepts data as input, processes it according to stored instructions, and produces meaningful output. It can also store data and results for future use.
questions.explanation: The definition must cover the four basic actions: accept input, process it, produce output and store data.

questions.question: What is data?
questions.modelAnswer: Data are raw, unprocessed facts and figures, such as numbers, words, images or sounds, that are fed into a computer.
questions.explanation: Data are raw facts; they become information only after processing.

questions.question: What is information?
questions.modelAnswer: Information is the meaningful and organised result obtained after processing data, which helps in understanding and decision making.
questions.explanation: Information is the useful output produced when raw data are processed.

questions.question: Write the full form of CPU.
questions.modelAnswer: CPU stands for Central Processing Unit. It is also called the processor or the brain of the computer.
questions.explanation: The CPU processes data and controls all other units, so it is called the brain of the computer.

questions.question: What is a bit?
questions.modelAnswer: A bit (binary digit) is the smallest unit of memory. It can store either a 0 or a 1.
questions.explanation: A bit is the smallest memory unit and represents one binary digit, 0 or 1.

questions.question: How many bits make one byte?
questions.modelAnswer: Eight bits make one byte. A byte is the standard unit used to store one character of text.
questions.explanation: A byte is defined as a group of 8 bits and usually stores one character.

questions.question: Define volatile memory.
questions.modelAnswer: Volatile memory is memory that loses its stored contents when the power is switched off. RAM is an example of volatile memory.
questions.explanation: Volatile memory keeps data only while power is on; RAM is the common example.

questions.question: What is firmware?
questions.modelAnswer: Firmware is permanent software stored in ROM that provides the basic instructions needed to start (boot) a computer, such as the BIOS.
questions.explanation: Firmware is stored in non-volatile ROM and is used to start the computer.

questions.question: What is an input device? Give one example.
questions.modelAnswer: An input device is a device used to enter data and instructions into a computer. For example, a keyboard.
questions.explanation: Input devices supply data to the computer; the keyboard is the most common example.

questions.question: What does MICR stand for?
questions.modelAnswer: MICR stands for Magnetic Ink Character Recognition. It is used in banks to read the magnetic ink characters printed on cheques.
questions.explanation: MICR reads characters printed with magnetic ink, mainly on bank cheques.

questions.question: Differentiate between data and information.
questions.modelAnswer: Data are raw, unprocessed facts, while information is processed data that is meaningful and useful. For example, the individual marks 45, 60 and 75 are data, and their average of 60 is information.
questions.explanation: The key idea is that processing turns raw data into useful information.

questions.question: Explain the role of the Control Unit in a computer.
questions.modelAnswer: The Control Unit fetches instructions from memory, decodes them and directs all other units to carry out the required operations. It coordinates the working of the ALU, memory and input/output units, so it is called the nerve centre of the computer.
questions.explanation: The Control Unit does not do calculations itself; it directs and synchronises all the other units.

questions.question: Why is RAM called volatile memory?
questions.modelAnswer: RAM is called volatile memory because it stores data only as long as the computer has power. When the power is switched off, all the contents of RAM are lost, which is why unsaved work disappears on an unexpected shutdown.
rubric: Contents lost when power is off
questions.explanation: Volatility means the memory does not retain data without a continuous power supply.

questions.question: State two differences between primary memory and secondary memory.
questions.modelAnswer: Primary memory is directly accessed by the CPU and is very fast but has a small capacity, while secondary memory is not directly accessed by the CPU and is slower but has a large capacity. Primary memory (RAM) is volatile, whereas secondary memory is non-volatile.
rubric: Direct vs indirect access by CPU
questions.explanation: Primary memory is close to the CPU and fast; secondary memory is larger, cheaper and permanent.

questions.question: Explain any three data capturing devices.
questions.modelAnswer: OMR (Optical Mark Recognition) reads the pencil marks made on objective answer sheets. OCR (Optical Character Recognition) converts a scanned image of printed text into editable digital text. MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition) reads the magnetic ink characters printed on bank cheques.
questions.explanation: These three devices capture specific kinds of printed or marked data automatically, saving time and reducing errors.

questions.question: What is the function of the ALU?
questions.modelAnswer: The ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) performs all arithmetic operations such as addition and subtraction, and all logical operations such as comparison of values. It is the part of the CPU that does the actual calculations.
rubric: Mentions it is part of the CPU
questions.explanation: The ALU handles both arithmetic and logic, so it is the calculation centre of the CPU.

questions.question: Explain Von Neumann architecture in brief.
questions.modelAnswer: In Von Neumann architecture, both data and instructions are stored in the same main memory. The CPU fetches one instruction at a time, decodes it and executes it. This fetch-decode-execute cycle is the basis of most modern computers.
rubric: Data and instructions in the same memory
questions.explanation: The stored-program concept, where instructions live in memory alongside data, is central to this architecture.

questions.question: What is cache memory and why is it used?
questions.modelAnswer: Cache is a small, very fast memory placed between the CPU and the main memory. It stores frequently used data and instructions so that the CPU can access them quickly, thereby reducing the average access time.
rubric: Located between CPU and main memory
questions.explanation: Cache bridges the speed gap between the very fast CPU and the slower main memory.

questions.question: List any four units of memory measurement in increasing order of size.
questions.modelAnswer: In increasing order the units are: bit, byte, kilobyte (KB), megabyte (MB), gigabyte (GB) and terabyte (TB). Among these, the bit is the smallest and the terabyte is the largest listed.
questions.explanation: Memory units grow in steps of 1024 in the binary convention, starting from the bit.

questions.question: State two differences between SRAM and DRAM.
questions.modelAnswer: SRAM (Static RAM) is faster and does not need to be refreshed continuously, but it is more expensive and is used as cache memory. DRAM (Dynamic RAM) is slower and must be refreshed continuously, but it is cheaper and is used as the main memory.
rubric: SRAM is faster and does not need refreshing
DRAM is slower and needs refreshing
questions.explanation: The two types of RAM differ in speed, cost and the need for refreshing, which decides where each is used.

questions.question: Explain the functional units of a computer with the help of a block diagram.
questions.modelAnswer: A computer has four main functional units. (1) Input Unit: it accepts data and instructions from the user and converts them into a computer-readable form; e.g. keyboard, mouse. (2) Central Processing Unit (CPU): it is the brain of the computer and has three parts - the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) which performs arithmetic and logical operations, the Control Unit (CU) which fetches and decodes instructions and controls all other units, and registers which hold data temporarily. (3) Memory Unit: it stores data, instructions and intermediate results; it is of two types, primary (RAM, ROM) and secondary (hard disk, pen drive). (4) Output Unit: it converts the processed result into a human-readable form; e.g. monitor, printer. A block diagram shows the input unit feeding the CPU, the CPU using the memory unit, and the CPU sending results to the output unit.
rubric: Names the four functional units (1 mark)
Explains input unit and output unit with examples (1 mark)
Explains the CPU with ALU, CU and registers (1.5 marks)
Explains the memory unit with examples (1 mark)
Draws a correct block diagram (0.5 mark)
questions.explanation: This question tests the overall structure of a computer; the block diagram and the three parts of the CPU carry most of the marks.

questions.question: Explain the five generations of computers, mentioning the main component of each.
questions.modelAnswer: First generation (1940-1956): used vacuum tubes; machines were very large, generated much heat and used machine language; e.g. ENIAC, UNIVAC. Second generation (1956-1963): used transistors, which were smaller, faster and more reliable; assembly language was used; e.g. IBM 1401. Third generation (1964-1971): used integrated circuits (ICs), making computers smaller and more reliable; keyboards and monitors were used and high-level languages appeared; e.g. IBM 360. Fourth generation (1971-present): used microprocessors (VLSI), which led to personal computers, graphical user interfaces and networks; e.g. IBM PC, Apple Macintosh. Fifth generation (present-future): uses artificial intelligence and parallel processing with voice recognition and smart assistants; e.g. IBM Watson. In general, each generation made computers smaller, faster, cheaper and able to store more data.
questions.explanation: Marks are usually given for correctly pairing each generation with its main component and one example.

questions.question: Explain primary memory and secondary memory with examples, and state any two differences between them.
questions.modelAnswer: Primary memory (main memory) is directly accessible to the CPU and holds the data and instructions currently being processed. It includes RAM and ROM. RAM is volatile and is used to store the running programs and their data, while ROM is non-volatile and stores permanent instructions such as firmware. Secondary memory (auxiliary memory) is not directly accessible to the CPU and is used for permanent storage of data and programs; examples are the hard disk, SSD, pen drive and DVD. Differences: (1) primary memory is directly accessed by the CPU while secondary memory is not; (2) primary memory is faster but smaller and costlier, whereas secondary memory is slower but larger and cheaper; also RAM in primary memory is volatile while secondary memory is non-volatile.
rubric: Defines primary memory with RAM and ROM examples (1.5 marks)
Defines secondary memory with examples (1.5 marks)
questions.explanation: The answer must clearly separate primary and secondary memory and support the differences with examples.

questions.question: Explain any five data capturing devices along with their applications.
questions.modelAnswer: Data capturing devices enter raw data into a computer. (1) Keyboard: used to type text and numbers. (2) Mouse: used for pointing, clicking and selecting items on the screen. (3) Scanner: converts printed documents and photographs into digital form. (4) OMR (Optical Mark Recognition): reads pencil marks, used to check objective answer sheets. (5) OCR (Optical Character Recognition): converts a scanned image of printed text into editable text, used to digitise books and documents. (6) MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition): reads magnetic ink characters, used by banks to process cheques. (7) Barcode reader: reads the barcodes on products, used at supermarket billing counters. Any five of these may be explained.
rubric: States a clear application for each (1 mark)
questions.explanation: Each device should be paired with a correct real-life application to score full marks.

questions.question: Explain the memory hierarchy and the basic units of memory measurement.
questions.modelAnswer: The memory hierarchy arranges memories from the fastest and smallest to the slowest and largest. In order, they are: registers (inside the CPU, fastest and smallest), cache, main memory (RAM and ROM), secondary memory (hard disk, SSD, DVD) and tertiary or cloud storage (slowest and largest). As we move down the hierarchy, speed and cost per unit decrease while capacity increases. The basic units of memory measurement are the bit (smallest, stores 0 or 1), byte (8 bits), kilobyte (1024 bytes), megabyte (1024 KB), gigabyte (1024 MB), terabyte (1024 GB) and petabyte (1024 TB). Note that storage manufacturers often use the decimal convention where 1 KB = 1000 bytes.
rubric: Correct order of the memory hierarchy (1.5 marks)
Explains speed and capacity trend down the hierarchy (1 mark)
Lists the units of measurement from bit to terabyte (1.5 marks)
questions.explanation: The hierarchy links speed, cost and capacity; the measurement units should be listed in increasing order.

questions.question: Working of a Personal Computer

caseStudy.passage: Riya switches on her home computer. She types her project report using the keyboard and sees it on the monitor. Inside the computer, the CPU processes her typing, and the RAM temporarily holds the open document. When she saves the file, it is written to the hard disk. The CPU performs the calculation for the word count, while another part of the CPU decides which instruction to run next.

subQuestions.question: Which unit temporarily holds the open document while Riya is working on it?
subQuestions.explanation: RAM is the volatile main memory that temporarily holds the data of the program currently in use.

subQuestions.question: Which part of the CPU performs the word-count calculation?
subQuestions.explanation: The Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) performs all arithmetic and logical operations, including counting.

subQuestions.question: Name the unit that decides which instruction to run next and coordinates the other units.
subQuestions.answer: The Control Unit. It fetches and decodes instructions and directs all the other units to carry out the required operations.
subQuestions.explanation: The Control Unit is the nerve centre that coordinates and controls every other unit.

subQuestions.question: Riya's saved file remains safe even after the computer is switched off. Name the type of memory that stores it and explain why.
subQuestions.answer: The file is stored on the hard disk, which is secondary memory. Secondary memory is non-volatile, so it keeps data permanently even when the power is switched off.
subQuestions.explanation: Non-volatile secondary memory retains data without power, unlike volatile RAM.

subQuestions.question: The keyboard and the monitor belong to which categories of units respectively?
subQuestions.explanation: The keyboard is an input device and the monitor is an output device.

questions.explanation: This case links everyday computer use to the functional units and to the idea of volatile and non-volatile memory.

questions.question: Choosing Storage Devices

caseStudy.passage: A school is buying computer parts. The table below lists the memories and storage devices considered, along with their capacities.

subQuestions.question: Which device in the table is volatile?
subQuestions.explanation: RAM is volatile; it loses its contents when power is switched off.

subQuestions.question: Convert the capacity of the pen drive (32 GB) into MB using the binary convention (1 GB = 1024 MB).
subQuestions.explanation: In the binary convention each step of 1 GB equals 1024 MB, so 32 GB = 32768 MB.

subQuestions.question: Which two devices in the table are primary memory?
subQuestions.explanation: Primary memory consists of RAM and ROM; hard disks and pen drives are secondary storage.

subQuestions.question: Give one reason why a hard disk is used to store files permanently instead of RAM.
subQuestions.answer: A hard disk is non-volatile secondary memory, so it keeps data even when the power is switched off, whereas RAM is volatile and loses its contents.
subQuestions.explanation: Permanent storage requires non-volatile memory, which RAM is not.

questions.explanation: This case tests the classification of memory and a simple unit conversion, and the link between volatility and permanent storage.

questions.question: Capturing Data in Daily Life

caseStudy.passage: At a supermarket, the cashier uses a barcode reader to read product codes. In a bank, a machine reads the numbers printed in magnetic ink on cheques. At a school, an OMR machine checks objective answer sheets, and in the office, a scanner with OCR software is used to convert printed letters into editable text.

subQuestions.question: Which technology is used at the supermarket billing counter to read product codes?
subQuestions.explanation: A barcode reader scans the black-and-white pattern of a barcode and converts it into digital data.

subQuestions.question: Which device is used in the bank to read the numbers printed on cheques?
subQuestions.explanation: MICR reads magnetic ink characters, which is why it is used on bank cheques.

subQuestions.question: When the office scans a printed letter and wants to edit its text, which technology is used? Explain briefly.
subQuestions.answer: OCR (Optical Character Recognition) is used. It converts the scanned image of printed text into editable digital text.
subQuestions.explanation: OCR recognises characters in a scanned image and turns them into machine-editable text.

subQuestions.question: Define data capturing and give one example from the passage.
subQuestions.answer: Data capturing is the process of entering raw data into a computer using input devices. Example: scanning a barcode at the supermarket.
subQuestions.explanation: Data capturing means feeding raw data into the computer through input devices.

questions.explanation: This case connects OMR, OCR, MICR and barcode readers to their real-world applications.
